title: Bench — Postgres
description: Shared bench Postgres 17 broken out per engine database, so each workflow engine's connection, throughput, cache and storage cost is attributable to it.

panels.title: Exporter up
panels.description: up{job="postgres"} — Prometheus scrape health of the postgres_exporter on bench-obs:9187. Down here means the panels below are stale, not that Postgres is down.

panels.title: Postgres up
panels.description: pg_up — the exporter's own connectivity check against the bench Postgres 17 instance in the bench-pg Incus container.

panels.title: Backends vs max_connections
panels.description: 100 * sum(pg_stat_database_numbackends) / scalar(pg_settings_max_connections). The engines share one 100-connection cluster, so this is the headroom left for adding another engine to the bench.

panels.title: Total database size
panels.description: sum(pg_database_size_bytes) over the engine databases (templates excluded). On-disk size as Postgres reports it, so it includes bloat not yet vacuumed.

panels.title: Postgres uptime
panels.description: time() - pg_postmaster_start_time_seconds from the postmaster collector. A reset here invalidates every cumulative counter on this dashboard, including the cache hit ratios, so check it before reading a run's numbers.

panels.title: Transactions/s (all databases)
panels.description: sum(rate(pg_stat_database_xact_commit[5m])) — committed transactions per second across every database. This is the bench's aggregate write pressure on the shared Postgres, which is the load bottleneck rather than the engines themselves.

panels.title: Backends by engine database
panels.description: pg_stat_database_numbackends by datname. One database per engine: temporal = Temporal main store, temporal_visibility = Temporal visibility store, hatchet = Hatchet, bench = Absurd, postgres = system database. Steady-state count is each engine's idle connection cost — Hatchet's pool cap is per pool and lite runs several, so it exceeds DATABASE_MAX_CONNS.

panels.title: Current backends by engine database
panels.description: pg_stat_database_numbackends, latest sample per datname. Direct read of each engine's steady-state connection footprint against the shared cluster.

panels.title: Total backends against the cap
panels.description: sum(pg_stat_database_numbackends) plotted against pg_settings_max_connections. The cap line is the cluster-wide limit every engine competes for.

panels.title: Backend states by engine database
panels.description: pg_stat_activity_count by datname and state. Idle-in-transaction growth is the signal worth watching: it holds locks and xmin without doing work.

panels.title: Longest running transaction
panels.description: pg_stat_activity_max_tx_duration by datname — age of the oldest open transaction. A rising line blocks vacuum and lets dead tuples accumulate.

panels.title: Commits/s by engine database
panels.description: rate(pg_stat_database_xact_commit[5m]) by datname. Attributes transaction volume to the engine that generated it.

panels.title: Rollbacks/s by engine database
panels.description: rate(pg_stat_database_xact_rollback[5m]) by datname. A steady non-zero rate is normal for engines that poll with optimistic locking; a step change is not.

panels.title: Rows returned and fetched/s
panels.description: rate(pg_stat_database_tup_returned[5m]) and tup_fetched by datname. Returned counts rows scanned, fetched counts rows actually handed back — a wide gap means sequential scanning.

panels.title: Rows written/s
panels.description: rate of pg_stat_database_tup_inserted / _updated / _deleted by datname. The write mix per engine; update- and delete-heavy engines generate the dead tuples that drive vacuum load.

panels.title: Deadlocks, conflicts and temp files
panels.description: rate of pg_stat_database_deadlocks, _conflicts and _temp_files by datname. Any deadlock is a contention finding attributable to one engine; temp files mean queries spilled past work_mem.

panels.title: Cache hit ratio by engine database
panels.description: 100 * blks_hit / (blks_hit + blks_read) from pg_stat_database, by datname. Cumulative since stats reset, so it moves slowly — treat a sustained dip below 95% as the working set outgrowing the 128 MiB shared_buffers.

panels.title: Current cache hit ratio
panels.description: Latest 100 * blks_hit / (blks_hit + blks_read) per datname. Below 95% is worth investigating; below 90% means the bench is measuring disk, not the engine.

panels.title: Block reads/s (cache misses)
panels.description: rate(pg_stat_database_blks_read[5m]) by datname — blocks fetched from outside shared_buffers. These may still be served by the host page cache, so this is a miss rate, not a disk I/O rate.

panels.title: Database size by engine
panels.description: pg_database_size_bytes by datname. Growth slope is a first-class bench signal: Temporal's event-history retention shows up here as steady growth in the temporal database while the others stay flat.

panels.title: Current database size
panels.description: pg_database_size_bytes, latest sample per datname. Storage cost of each engine's steady state.

panels.title: Largest tables by engine
panels.description: pg_table_total_bytes with its heap and index components, from the textfile poller on bench-obs (job node, sampled every 5 min). Total includes indexes and TOAST, so Total minus Heap minus Indexes is TOAST. The poller publishes the top 15 tables per database by design — the engine schemas have a long tail of tiny tables, so this is a deliberate cut, not a truncated list.

panels.title: Table growth — largest tables across all engines
panels.description: topk(12, pg_table_total_bytes) over time. This is where an engine's retention behaviour becomes visible per relation: Temporal's history_node and executions_visibility grow with event history, Hatchet's dated OLAP partitions appear and roll over. Steps are 5 minutes wide because that is the poll interval.

panels.title: Tracked table bytes by engine
panels.description: sum by (datname) of pg_table_total_bytes — the top-15 tables per database summed. This is deliberately less than pg_database_size_bytes: it excludes the long tail, system catalogs and free space, so use it for composition and the database-size panels above for absolute footprint.

panels.title: Dead tuples by table
panels.description: Dead tuples per table, from the pg-table-metrics poller rather than from postgres_exporter: its stat_user_tables collector is per-connection and the exporter DSN names the postgres database, which holds no user tables. The poller already connects to each engine database for the size queries, so the vacuum counters ride along. A line climbing with no autovacuum behind it is bloat forming; pair it with pg_table_last_autovacuum_timestamp_seconds.

panels.title: Table poller up
panels.description: pg_table_poller_up — 1 when the textfile poller reached every engine database on its last run. When this is 0 the size breakdown panels are stale rather than empty, because the textfile collector keeps re-publishing the previous values.

panels.title: Locks by engine database and mode
panels.description: pg_locks_count by datname and mode. Only non-zero modes are drawn — the exporter emits a zero series for every mode on every database.

panels.title: Current locks by mode
panels.description: sum by (mode) of pg_locks_count across the engine databases, non-zero only. rowexclusivelock and exclusivelock climbing together indicate queue contention.

panels.title: Blocked sessions
panels.description: AWAITS FUTURE METRIC: no waiting/blocked series exists — pg_locks_count reports granted locks only and pg_stat_activity_count has no wait_event dimension in this exporter. Blocked-session counts need a custom query over pg_locks WHERE NOT granted, supplied through the exporter's runConfigFile queries file. The closest available proxy, sessions stuck idle in transaction, is charted below.

panels.title: Buffer allocation and background writes/s
panels.description: rate of pg_stat_bgwriter_buffers_alloc_total and _buffers_clean_total. Allocation rate is buffer churn in the 128 MiB shared_buffers; clean is what the background writer flushed. Cluster-wide, not attributable per engine.

panels.title: bgwriter maxwritten stops/s
panels.description: rate(pg_stat_bgwriter_maxwritten_clean_total[5m]) — how often the background writer hit bgwriter_lru_maxpages and stopped early, pushing flush work onto backends. Non-zero means the writer is undersized for the load.

panels.title: WAL archiver
panels.description: pg_stat_archiver_archived_count and _failed_count. The bench cluster runs without archiving, so a flat zero here is the expected reading and any movement means configuration drifted.

panels.title: Checkpoint rate
panels.description: rate of pg_stat_checkpointer_num_timed_total, _num_requested_total and _buffers_written_total from the stat_checkpointer collector, which is where Postgres 17 keeps these counters. Timed checkpoints fire on checkpoint_timeout; requested ones mean max_wal_size was hit first, which is the signal that write volume outran the WAL budget.

panels.title: Checkpoint time share
panels.description: rate of pg_stat_checkpointer_write_time_total and _sync_time_total, both cumulative milliseconds, divided by 1000 to read as a fraction of wall-clock time. Write time is high by design because checkpoint_completion_target deliberately spreads the flush; sync time rising is the one that indicates storage is struggling.

panels.title: WAL directory size
panels.description: pg_wal_size_bytes and pg_wal_segments from the wal collector, which reads pg_ls_waldir. This is the current on-disk size of pg_wal, not cumulative WAL volume — segments are recycled, so the line sawtooths against max_wal_size rather than climbing. Segments are 16 MiB each.

panels.title: Exporter collector health
panels.description: pg_scrape_collector_success by collector — 1 when that collector's queries succeeded on the last scrape. A collector that drops to 0 silently empties whichever panels depend on it, so this is the first place to look when a section goes blank. The exporter connects as the bench_exporter role holding pg_monitor, which is what the wal and postmaster collectors require.

panels.title: WAL generation rate
panels.description: Cluster-wide WAL actually written, from pg_stat_wal via the pg-table-metrics poller. postgres_exporter's wal collector reads pg_ls_waldir instead, which describes the directory as it stands and sawtooths as segments recycle, so a rate over it is not a write rate. This is the bench's cross-engine write-amplification measure. It is cluster-wide, not per database — attribute it by running one engine at a time.
